fields.expected: Most of my recent work has been about agents that touch real systems and where automation should stop. I built a Playwright-based job-application agent in TypeScript with SQLite as the single source of truth, an explicit state machine from DISCOVERED through SUBMITTED, and fail-closed flags like SUBMIT_ENABLED that never default on. Free-text essays and demographic fields are architecturally prevented from being auto-filled, because a wrong action there is a real application submitted with a fabricated answer. I also intentionally skip Workday and iCIMS rather than handle them unreliably. Sierra is building agents that talk to actual customers of companies like Uber, CLEAR, and Sutter Health, which means the same problem at much higher stakes: the agent has to be useful and it has to be right, and you need a way to know which one it is before it ships. Evaluation is the part I would most want to work on. At Intelehealth I designed a framework comparing LLM-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case standard using stratified sampling to surface systematic failure modes, and that convinced me judging an output is harder than generating one.

fields.expected:
I think a great agent engineer treats reliability as the actual product. Anyone can get an agent to work once against a fixture; the hard part is knowing when it is safe to act, what it should refuse to do, and how you would prove it works before a real customer is on the other end. That means caring about state, failure modes, and evaluation as much as prompting.

My job-application agent is the clearest evidence I have. I built a validation ladder, UNIT_CONFIRMED to FIXTURE_CONFIRMED to LIVE_READ_ONLY_CONFIRMED to LIVE_MUTATION_CONFIRMED, because a capability should only claim the level of reality it has actually been tested against. I supported Greenhouse fully and Lever and Ashby partially, and deliberately detected and skipped Workday, iCIMS, and Oracle rather than handling them unreliably. I also built an operator console so a human could observe and approve each step.

Evaluation is the other half. At Intelehealth I designed a framework comparing LLM-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case standard using stratified sampling to surface systematic failure modes. That work convinced me generating an answer is cheap and deciding whether to trust it is the real engineering problem, which is exactly what customer-facing agents live and die on.

fields.expected:
Two things that don't fit neatly into the other answers. First, most of what I've built has had to survive contact with real users, not just a demo. I co-founded Open Health Intelligence and built ClarityAtlas end to end in Swift and SwiftUI, including a passive sleep-estimation system using HealthKit and Core Motion signals so users didn't need a wearable, and we shipped it into a live Hopkins pilot with 30+ users. Getting it in front of people mattered as much as the code. My cofounders and I once knocked on the doors of Garland Hall until we got to pitch President Daniels, which eventually became a formal meeting.

Second, I've spent the past year independently researching how research institutions select and evaluate uncertain work, talking to researchers, administrators, and science-policy people. The question I keep landing on is that as AI makes generation cheap, judgment becomes the bottleneck. That is the same question I see in agents: producing a response is easy, deciding whether it should be trusted and sent is the hard part. I'd like to work on that with people who have real customers depending on the answer.
